name: Glimepiride
mechanism: Binds to SUR1 subunit of ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channels on pancreatic beta cells, causing channel closure → membrane depolarization → calcium influx → insulin granule exocytosis. Stimulates insulin release from functioning beta cells. Requires some endogenous insulin production. Also extrapancreatic effects (↑ peripheral insulin sensitivity, ↓ hepatic glucose output)
dosing: Start 1mg PO OD with breakfast (or first main meal). Titrate gradually (1mg increments) every 1-2 weeks based on blood glucose. Usual maintenance: 1-4mg daily. Max 6mg daily (some say 8mg). Single daily dose. Reduce in renal impairment (eGFR <30: start 0.5mg, cautious titration; eGFR <15: avoid - hypoglycaemia risk). Elderly: start 0.5-1mg (higher hypoglycaemia risk)
contraindications: Type 1 diabetes (no beta cells), diabetic ketoacidosis. Severe renal impairment (eGFR <15, dialysis - prolonged hypoglycaemia risk). Severe hepatic impairment. Hypersensitivity to sulfonamides. Caution: G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk), elderly (hypoglycaemia), moderate renal impairment (dose reduce)
interactions: Alcohol: ↑ hypoglycaemia risk (also disulfiram-like reaction). Beta-blockers: mask hypoglycaemia symptoms (tachycardia, tremor). Drugs ↑ hypoglycaemia risk: insulin, other antidiabetics, NSAIDs, fibrates, ACE inhibitors, fluconazole, sulfonamides, clarithromycin. Drugs ↓ glucose-lowering effect: thiazides, corticosteroids, thyroid hormones, oral contraceptives, phenytoin, sympathomimetics. Warfarin: unpredictable INR changes (monitor). Rifampicin: ↓ glimepiride levels
monitoring: Fasting blood glucose (FBG) and/or HbA1c (every 3-6 months - target <53mmol/mol usually). Hypoglycaemia (symptoms, frequency, severity - especially elderly, renal impairment). Weight (usually modest gain 1-2kg). Renal function (annual, more if impaired - dose adjustment). Adherence. Cardiovascular risk factors (BP, lipids). Signs of beta-cell failure (inadequate glycaemic control despite max dose - consider insulin)
pregnancy: AVOID - switch to insulin. Sulfonylureas cross placenta → risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia (prolonged), possible teratogenicity (controversial). Insulin preferred for glycaemic control in pregnancy. Discontinue 2-4 weeks before conception if planned pregnancy
sideEffects: Common: hypoglycaemia (especially missed meals, excess alcohol, renal impairment, elderly - can be severe/prolonged). Weight gain (~1-3kg, less than other SUs). GI upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort). Uncommon: rash, pruritus, photosensitivity. Rare: hepatotoxicity (cholestatic jaundice, transaminase elevation), blood dyscrasias (thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, agranulocytosis - stop if develops), hyponatraemia (SIADH), hypersensitivity reactions, haemolytic anaemia (G6PD deficiency). Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (flushing, N&V)
pharmacokinetics: Well absorbed orally. Peak 2-3h. Protein-bound (>99%). Hepatically metabolized by CYP2C9 to active and inactive metabolites. Half-life: 5-9h (longer duration of action - 24h, allows once-daily dosing). Excreted: 60% urine, 40% faeces (metabolites). Accumulates in renal impairment (prolonged hypoglycaemia)
clinicalPearls: Second-generation sulfonylurea. Similar efficacy to gliclazide but LONGER duration (24h, once-daily). Advantages: once-daily dosing (better adherence), less weight gain than some SUs, lower hypoglycaemia risk than older SUs (glibenclamide). Disadvantages: still causes hypoglycaemia and weight gain (more than metformin/DPP-4i/GLP-1RA), cardiovascular neutrality (UKPDS: no CV benefit vs insulin). PLACE IN THERAPY: second-line (or third-line) after metformin in T2DM if target not met. Consider if: metformin contraindicated/intolerant, additional glucose-lowering needed. Alternatives often preferred: DPP-4i (vildagliptin, sitagliptin - no hypoglycaemia/weight gain), SGLT2i (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin - CV/renal benefits), GLP-1RA (liraglutide, dulaglutide - weight loss, CV benefits). SUs declining in use (hypoglycaemia, weight gain, ? CV safety concerns, beta-cell exhaustion). HYPOGLYCAEMIA: main concern. Risk factors: elderly, renal impairment, erratic meals, alcohol, polypharmacy. Educate patients: symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, confusion), treatment (15-20g fast-acting CHO - glucose tablets, juice, then complex CHO), avoid if meal delayed. CARRY glucose/snacks. Prolonged hypoglycaemia: glimepiride half-life 5-9h but duration 24h - hypoglycaemia can be prolonged, requiring IV glucose, observation. RENAL IMPAIRMENT: dose reduce if eGFR <60, cautious if <30, avoid if <15 (accumulation, prolonged hypoglycaemia). Alternative: DPP-4i (most OK in renal impairment), insulin (adjust dose). DUAL THERAPY: metformin + glimepiride common. Triple therapy: add SGLT2i, DPP-4i, or insulin. MAX DOSE: if inadequate control on 4-6mg glimepiride + metformin, consider adding third agent or switching to insulin (beta-cell failure). WEIGHT: causes 1-3kg gain (less than glibenclamide, more than metformin). If weight concern, prefer SGLT2i or GLP-1RA. CV SAFETY: neutral (CAROLINA trial vs linagliptin - non-inferior). No CV benefit like SGLT2i/GLP-1RA. ONCE-DAILY: take with breakfast or first main meal (requires food intake to match insulin release, ↓ hypoglycaemia risk). Don't skip meals. ALTERNATIVES WITHIN SU CLASS: gliclazide (similar, BD dosing, MR formulation available), glibenclamide (older, higher hypoglycaemia risk - avoid). Glimepiride vs gliclazide: similar efficacy, glimepiride once-daily (better adherence), gliclazide lower hypoglycaemia (ADVANCE trial). STOPPING: if inadequate control (HbA1c >58-64 despite max dual therapy), consider insulin. If remission (weight loss, lifestyle), may be able to stop (review regularly)
indication: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (second/third-line, usually with metformin, when diet/exercise/metformin inadequate)
